candidates: A broader alternate reading is that the feature responds to technical/metadata contexts containing a `label` field or tag name across markup/config syntaxes, but this is secondary to simply seeing the token `label`.

The feature is primarily a lexical detector for the exact word `label`, with only a weak secondary preference for code/annotation formatting such as `label{key}` or `label=value`; the formatting itself is not necessary.
The feature fires on the literal string/token `label`, especially in technical or markup-like text where `label` appears verbatim (e.g. `\\label{...}`, `<label>`, quoted/code mentions of `label`).

Feature fires at a begin-of-sequence/document-boundary token that marks the start of a new, standalone text segment after unrelated preceding content; it is especially common when the new segment opens like a title, heading, prompt, or other abrupt document start.
Feature may specialize to BOS followed by heading-like or title-case document openings, such as article titles, section headers, chapter names, or metadata-style standalone names.
Feature may also respond to BOS followed by short formatted prompt/metadata prefixes, e.g. 'Q:', 'A:', 'Title:', 'Summary:', or similar abrupt labeled starts of a new segment.

Activates on near-literal mentions of the Go module path `github.com/Azure/go-autorest/autorest/...`, especially continuations under that path such as `/azure`, `/adal`, `/to`, or similar import/package references.

A narrower sub-sense may prefer the exact GitHub-style prefix `github.com/Azure/go-autorest/autorest/` rather than generic mentions of 'Azure autorest'; activation seems driven by the repository/import-path surface form more than by semantics.

Possible secondary memorized phrase sense: exact or very close surface forms around `collected from various sites of ...`, but only as a brittle lexical fragment rather than a productive semantic concept.
Activates on decorative or prominent document headings containing a letter-spaced all-caps title, often with surrounding divider lines, but the divider lines are not required.

Activates on visually segmented all-caps section/header text where letters are separated character-by-character, including spaced forms and sometimes punctuation-separated forms like "R-E-S-U-L-T-S" or partial-separated forms such as "A - P P E N D I X".
Activates on words or short labels written in all caps with spaces between individual letters, especially heading-like text such as "T E S T S", "O P I N I O N", or "O R D E R".

Feature is currently unsupported by probes; the safest revision is that it may key on dataset-specific corruption where a token fragment is inserted between literal `<<` and `>>` inside otherwise technical text, especially in math/code/biomedical strings such as `BHLH1<<0>>1`, `\<<alpha>>`, or `a_{<<1>>3}`.

Possible polysemantic alternative: feature responds to broken technical identifiers where a short fragment like a digit, Greek-name piece, or stem (`0`, `1`, `alpha`, `own`) is split out from a larger token by surrounding punctuation/formatting boundaries.

Possible narrower math/code-table context feature: malformed serialized technical text containing quoting or escaping plus field/name fragments, e.g. LaTeX/control-sequence text, SQL/backticked column names, or indexed algebraic expressions that have been interrupted by annotation markers.
The feature fires on punctuation immediately before LaTeX/math content, especially colon or comma right before a `$...$` span or a TeX control sequence.

The feature detects boundary formatting around highly symbolic tokens: punctuation such as comma/colon placed directly before TeX/math expressions, and more weakly before other symbolic literals like hex constants.
A narrower subfeature may fire on delimiter tokens themselves at the start or edge of symbolic spans, especially `$` and punctuation+backslash sequences like `,\\`.
Semicolon after a generic collection-typed field declaration inside a class, e.g. `ArrayList<T> x;`, `List<T> x;`, or similar container/map fields.
Semicolon at the end of a simple class field declaration, with extra affinity for declarations immediately followed by another member declaration such as a constructor, method, or factory.
Semicolon ending a class-body field/member variable declaration, especially a bare declaration without an initializer like `private Type name;`.

Java/C#-style method declaration where `get` begins a camelCase method name, especially after modifiers plus a nontrivial return type, e.g. `private final User getOwner()` / `public static boolean getReady()` / `protected List getItems()`.
The feature prefers declaration/signature context for `getX(...)`, not prose or call sites: `get` must be the start of a method name in source code rather than just mentioned text.

The feature is selective within getter declarations: it fires more for getters with richer typed prefixes/return types (object, collection, boolean, modifiers like `private final`/`static`) and may miss very plain forms such as `public String getName()` or `private int getCount()`.
The middle/interior region of an unusually long punctuation-only span, particularly within a long hyphen border line rather than on normal prose mentions of dashes or hyphens.
Long ASCII separator/border lines made mostly of hyphens, often adjacent to headers or table-like structured text.
A highly specific ASCII-art divider containing the motif '<<---------------->>', especially when embedded inside much longer runs of hyphens.

Activates on URL-like slash-delimited web path strings, especially when a host or site/resource name is followed by multiple hierarchical path segments (e.g. example.com/docs/getting-started, forum.net/thread/48291/replies, api.service.io/v1/users/list).

Activates on hierarchical web paths containing compact identifier-like segments after slashes, such as versions, years, numeric IDs, or short codes (e.g. /v2/, /2024/, /11143/, /latest/, /atc10/), especially inside URL/path-like strings.
Activates at the boundary where a web host/domain-like token transitions into a slash-separated path, including URL-like hostnames, localhost, or service names followed by deeper directories/files.

The feature fires on the discourse marker "I think" when it is used by the speaker to introduce an upcoming proposition/opinion, typically at the start of a clause (e.g. "I think we should...", "I think that's...").
The feature may weakly generalize to first-person tentative opinion statements, but its core trigger is specifically the speaker phrase "I think" rather than uncertainty language in general.

A narrower variant: the feature is especially sensitive to the exact local string "I think" immediately followed by clause-onset material such as "that", "that's", pronouns, modals, or quantifiers ("I think this...", "I think we...", "I think most...").

The feature detects the literal substring/token "artist", especially when it appears as a metadata/schema label or identifier in structured text such as JSON keys/values, config fields, and machine-readable records (e.g. type/category/field names like "artist", "artist_id").

The feature is primarily lexical: it fires on the exact substring "artist" across many contexts, with boosted activation in structured or metadata-like environments; near-matches such as "artisan" are much weaker, while words containing the same character sequence like "artistry" can still partially trigger it.
A strong sub-case of the feature is "artist" inside machine-readable resource paths or URIs, especially artist endpoints/resource identifiers such as "/artist/12345-Name" and escaped variants.

The feature may detect corpus-concatenation boundaries: the transition from arbitrary prior text into an unrelated new document beginning at <<bos>>, regardless of domain, with many observed examples happening to be article abstracts, listings, news items, or patent-style openings.

A weaker alternate view is that the feature responds to BOS-prefixed document-openers that have entry/header-like surface form, such as titles, named entries, or abstract openings—but only in conjunction with the sequence-start context, not those forms in ordinary prose.

The feature keys primarily on the special beginning-of-sequence token/context (<<bos>>) that marks a new document/snippet, rather than on any specific semantic topic. It often appears strongest when the new span begins with standalone-entry or title-like opening prose.

Baseball inning-reference syntax: the feature fires on play-by-play/recap phrases where an inning is named with an ordinal, especially in templates like 'in the fifth', 'the bottom of the eighth', 'the top of the ninth', or 'to start the 10th'.
A narrower subfeature for baseball event-start phrasing with an inning mention, especially constructions like 'start the 10th', 'begin the ninth', or 'begins the bottom of the eighth'.

Concise baseball recap sentences containing a preposition or light verb followed by 'the' + ordinal inning phrase, e.g. 'in the fourth', 'in the seventh', 'before the bottom of the fifth', or 'to start the 10th'.

Broad polysemantic feature centered on the verb "settle" across two main senses: (1) resolve/decide/bring closure to disputes or questions, and (2) become established in a place or life situation ("settle in/down").
Uses of the verb "settle" meaning to resolve or bring closure to a dispute, argument, lawsuit, or open question.
Uses of "settle" meaning to establish oneself in a place or state of residence, including "settle in," "settle down," and migration/resettlement contexts.

A narrower subfeature: nouns denoting scalar settings, thresholds, counts, or resource levels when they appear as the object of explicit modification verbs such as increase, lower, cut, raise, or extend.

The feature fires on the noun phrase that is the target of a change/adjustment action: a controllable parameter, limit, resource, or scope being increased, lowered, cut, extended, raised, or diversified (e.g. temperature, deadline, dosage, speed limit, battery life, applicability, receptive field, number, offering).

A possible technical/formal-register variant: abstract system properties or configurable technical quantities being adjusted or referenced, especially in scientific, engineering, or platform-policy contexts (operating temperature, receptive field, reputation threshold, applicability, part number).

The feature fires on comma-formatted threshold/cutoff numbers that end in ',001' (or closely related bracket-boundary values), especially in policy, pricing, tax, or eligibility text such as '$150,001' or '75,001 units'.
A weaker secondary sense is dense numeric interval/mapping notation where punctuation is directly attached to digits, especially forms like '3--5', '1--2', or '7→9' in tabular/range text.
The feature may prefer boundary-number lists or threshold sequences centered on exact +1 cutoffs, such as '99,999, 100,000, and 100,001', rather than arbitrary large comma numbers.

More specifically, the feature prefers generic statistic-style or habitual-frequency claims in which "someone" is presented as an unspecified recurring victim of harm (e.g. 'Someone is harmed every year', 'Someone becomes a victim daily').

Weak possible secondary component for report-like factual lead-ins or emphatic transitions before statistics/findings (e.g. 'Remarkably, the study found...'), but this component is low-confidence and much less specific than the main 'someone victimization' feature.
Activates on sentence-initial generic statements about harm/crime/victimization that use the indefinite human pronoun "someone" as the subject (e.g. "Someone is assaulted...").

The feature activates on capitalized surname-like token continuations or uncommon last names in news-style attribution contexts, especially around verbs like said/says/denied after punctuation or quotes.

The feature detects unusual capitalized name pieces/subtokens, especially continuations that complete a surname after an initial fragment (e.g. <<ahn>> in K<<ahn>>, <<iano>> in M<<iano>>), rather than ordinary whole words.
The feature may be a boundary-sensitive detector for the start of a capitalized rare name or name-fragment immediately after quote/sentence punctuation, particularly in reported-speech/news text.
A narrower polysemantic component may respond to member-access/code tokens like `this.` at the beginning of a fresh code statement, especially near chunk starts or line/statement boundaries.
The feature may specifically detect text immediately following `<<<bos>>>` when the new chunk begins in a distinctive register such as code, legal/news boilerplate, citations, or markup/comments.
Activation is driven by a hard document/chunk boundary token, especially the exact start-of-sequence marker `<<<bos>>>` or an equivalent abrupt reset into unrelated text.
Token-boundary wordpieces that begin with uppercase 'Z', especially rare proper names, brands, and technical identifiers (e.g. Zuck, Zillow, ZTE, ZEB1/ZEB2, ZURB, ZSCAN).
A subfeature for token-boundary rare names/brands starting with 'Zu' or 'Zur', especially strings like Zuck, Zuckerberg, Zurich, and Zurb.
A subfeature for rare uppercase-Z technical/gene/computing identifiers, especially all-caps or mixed alphanumeric labels such as ZEB1, ZEB2, ZNF143, ZSCAN, and ZSCAN4.

Digits serving as page/pinpoint locators inside formal citation syntax—especially legal or bibliographic patterns like 'at 237', 'p. 128', '347 U.S. 483, 495', or 'supra note 4'—rather than ordinary narrative numbers.

Numbers in compact citation/page-reference notation, especially when introduced by citation markers or delimiters such as 'p.', 'pp.', 'at', colons, commas, or parentheses, e.g. 'p. 47', '2004: 112-13', '(1998), pp. 5-7'.
A narrower subcase: numbers inside parenthetical citation blocks that include an internal page/volume locator, such as '(Smith, 2019, p. 83)' or '(Brown, vol. 2:45)'.
JSX component configuration syntax in opening tags for framework-specific props such as `keyExtractor` and `store`, particularly in React/React Native.
JSX opening tags with prop assignments, especially expression-valued props written as `prop={...}` inside a component tag.
React/React Native component tags containing callback or object-valued props in braces, e.g. `keyExtractor={fn}`, `onPress={...}`, `options={{...}}`, `store={...}`.
Historical references to escaped, former, or enslaved people in 18th-19th century slavery contexts, especially abolition/Civil War-era U.S. prose.
American chattel slavery, especially references to people in relation to slave status or slaveholding: escaped/former/enslaved people and people who owned slaves.
Phrases about slaveholding or ownership of enslaved people/slaves.

Sentence-initial anticipatory 'it' in advisory extraposition: patterns like 'It may/might/would be useful/helpful/easier/best/wise/prudent to VERB,' expressing an impersonal recommendation or planning advice.
A narrower lexical phrase family centered on 'it may be useful to ...' and close recommendation variants such as 'it might be helpful to', 'it may be easier to', or 'it may be best to'.
Impersonal copular recommendation with evaluative adjective plus infinitive, including non-modal forms like 'It is convenient/advisable to VERB' in procedural or expository text.
May also respond more strongly when multiple spelled-out month-day-year dates appear in a sequence or list separated by commas/semicolons.
Activates on full month names that begin a written American-style date expression ('Month Day, Year'), regardless of surrounding sentence context.

Activates on full month names at the start of a spelled-out date in the form 'Month Day, Year', especially when the date is formatted as a standalone entry or follows punctuation/newlines in records, headers, or legal-style documents.

Sentence- or clause-initial contracted "That’s/that's", especially immediately after punctuation, quotes, or a newline; the feature is about the discourse-opening token pattern more than the specific meaning of the predicate.
A narrower subcase: clause-initial "That’s" used for short corrective/evaluative/summing-up statements such as "That’s not the point," "That’s exactly the problem," or "That’s all ...".
Capitalized contracted "That’s" in dialogue-like prose, with preference for utterance-initial position in quoted or narrative speech contexts.

The feature is especially common in public-facing announcement or community-address discourse where a speaker/group expresses positive sentiment before an infinitive, e.g. 'thrilled to announce', 'delighted to welcome', 'glad to see', 'proud to be part of', 'excited to share'.

The feature activates on the infinitival marker 'to' when it follows a positive-affect or honor adjective/participle expressing pleasure, pride, gratitude, or excitement, as in 'thrilled to', 'delighted to', 'glad to', 'proud to', 'fortunate to'.

The feature prefers evaluative-emotive adjective + infinitive constructions, often but not only in first person, and is weaker or less clean for person-specific framing; examples include 'I’m happy to', 'she was excited to', 'we’re delighted to'.
Hyphenated “-wide” compounds, especially forms like “system-wide”/“city-wide” where the feature may target the second piece “wide” or the whole hyphenated construction.
A very specific memorized token-context around the phrase break “onto the” across a newline, rather than a general feature for the token “the” after prepositions.

A sparse polysemantic feature for rare boundary continuations after punctuation/hyphen/newline, with strongest evidence on hyphenated “-wide” compounds and possibly another isolated memorized newline continuation.

Mentions of named defense contractors and official U.S. defense institutions/agencies, especially entities like General Dynamics, Lockheed Martin, Raytheon, Northrop Grumman, the Pentagon, or the Department of Defense in factual prose.

Named entities from the military-industrial / defense procurement world appearing in biographical or contract-reporting text, especially company names plus defense-bureaucracy entities in the same sentence.
Defense-sector employment or affiliation language involving a named defense organization, especially verbs like joined, hired by, work for, or accepted a post at a contractor or defense department.
Chemical nomenclature containing explicit stereochemical descriptors in or around parentheses near a hyphenated name, especially R/S locant assignments and related stereochemical annotations.
Organic-chemistry locanted stereochemistry lists in parentheses: comma-separated chiral assignments like '(1S,4R,5S)', often in names such as 'rel-(1S,4R,5S)-...' or directly before a compound name.
Relative stereochemistry notation with the prefix 'rel-' followed by an explicit parenthesized stereocenter assignment list, e.g. 'rel-(1R,3S,4S)-'.

The feature may more broadly detect standalone jurisdiction/place names in reportorial/legal-news contexts, especially around governmental or institutional predicates, whether or not a comma immediately follows.

The feature fires on a comma right after a standalone place/jurisdiction or institution-location noun phrase in formal/news prose, especially city/place names and location-based institutions (e.g. 'Schenectady,' 'Albany Medical Center,').
The feature is not a generic appositive/title-person comma feature; at most it weakly prefers certain state/place-title constructions like 'New York Governor,'.

A surface-pattern detector for the token sequence 'used/use ... to', centered on the past-habitual 'used to' phrase but with some spillover to nearby lexical patterns involving 'used' plus 'to' (e.g. 'used the key to...', 'be used to').

Detects the past habitual/former-state construction 'used to' (including informal 'use to'), especially when describing something that was true before but is no longer true, as in 'used to be/live/do/call'.

A narrower detector for 'used to' in contrastive before-vs-now statements about states, properties, or situations, especially clauses like 'X used to be...' or descriptions of how a place/object/relationship felt or was before.
Bibliographic reference fragments with compact journal/volume/page formatting, especially patterns like Journal 12(4):233-239, Nature 418:133-136, or 6:45-51, 2004.

Dense scholarly-reference punctuation-and-digit clusters, including DOI/article-number style fragments combined with commas, semicolons, parentheses, and page spans, e.g. '(2020), 8(4):233-241, doi:10.x'.
Citation-like page-range spans embedded in reference metadata, especially hyphenated numeric ranges after a colon or issue marker, such as 7(3):1810-1817 or vol. 4, pages 88-93.
Hyphenated or compound-modifier constructions built from a city, comma, and state abbreviation, such as "Austin, TX-based", "Miami, FL-area", or "Denver, CO-trained".

Scientific/vendor affiliation or address formatting containing a city, comma, and two-letter state abbreviation, often followed by additional address punctuation such as ", USA", semicolons, parentheses, or ZIP codes.
City name followed by a comma and a two-letter uppercase U.S. state abbreviation, especially in citation/address-style location strings (e.g. "Boston, MA", often with nearby punctuation or ZIP/USA).
A feature for title-cased multi-word names where a later component starts with "Ph", especially Vietnamese toponyms like "Tân Phước" and "Cúc Phương" including concatenated wiki-style forms.
An orthographic feature for a capitalized Vietnamese-style name component beginning with "Ph", especially in place names or surnames (e.g. Tân Phước, Mỹ Phước, Cẩm Phả, Phan Rang, Phạm).
A weak orthographic detector for the letter sequence/phonetic onset "ph" in romanized Vietnamese-looking tokens, with capitalization boosting activation but exact lexical identity not required.

The feature responds to enthusiastic scenic-view descriptions, especially landscapes/panoramas described with strong positive adjectives like awe-inspiring, majestic, breathtaking, stunning, or beautiful.
The feature is especially boosted by the phrase pattern 'awe-inspiring' or 'awe inspiring' when used to describe a landscape, panorama, vista, or scene.
The feature may partially key on positive evaluative words like 'inspiring' in descriptive contexts, but only weakly unless tied to scenic grandeur.
Formal technical/admin alert prose about system or hardware health/status notifications—e.g., warnings, notices, or messages concerning servers, storage, backup jobs, RAID, nodes, or cluster health.
Narrow collocation around 'important messages about' in manuals or warning sections, especially when followed by safety, installation, maintenance, or system topics.
Documentation/manual phrasing where 'messages about' introduces the subject of operational or maintenance notifications, especially in IT/admin contexts.
A token boundary around punctuation in code/math expressions, especially immediately before member-access dots or underscores, as in `uv.x`, `c2.r`, and `_thread_id`.
The special marker token `<<<bos>>>` / beginning-of-sequence boundary, particularly when introducing a new document-like segment such as a Q/A header or comment block.
Whitespace immediately before a hexadecimal literal `0x...` in code-like or structured text, e.g. `cur: 0xf3`, `idx: 0x4`, `addr: 0xbeef`.

A stronger subcase: instructional or constraining formulations like "in such a way/manner" and "in a way/manner that ...," especially when specifying how something should be arranged, phrased, modified, or organized.

Adverbial prepositional phrases of the form "in a/such a ... way" or "in a/such a ... manner," where "way/manner" is a generic method noun modified by an adjective or determiner and the whole phrase describes how an action is performed.

Abstract style/evaluative uses of the same construction, including phrases like "in a detached way," "in an intellectual manner," "in a professional manner," and polarity-sensitive variants like "in any way," where the phrase comments on manner, degree, or scope rather than concrete physical procedure.
JavaScript `console.log(...)` call syntax, especially the literal member-access pattern `console.log(` used to print a value or message.
JavaScript/HTML script debugging statements that log a variable or expression via `console.log(...)`, e.g. `console.log(data)` or `console.log('debug:', value)`.

JavaScript callback or handler snippets containing `console.log(...)`, such as `function(x){ console.log(x); }` or `x => console.log(x)`, but only as a secondary/contextual pattern rather than the core feature.

More specifically, the feature prefers metric distance/mass units written in full after Arabic numerals, with strongest support for forms like 'X meters', 'X meter', 'X grams', and 'X kilograms'; abbreviated units ('g', 'km', 'mm') and written-out numbers are weaker or inconsistent.

Explicit Arabic numeral + spelled-out metric unit expressions, especially distance and mass units such as '12 meters', '250 grams', and '3 kilograms', often in technical/scientific measurement wording. The activation is likely on the unit token immediately following the number.

The feature may have a secondary technical-measurement context component: quantitative scientific prose containing numeric measurements can weakly activate it, but this appears subordinate to the main trigger of digit + spelled-out metric unit.

Compact product/specification tokens: concrete numeric measurements, ratings, or model-size strings written in dense number+unit form in catalog/hardware text (e.g., 120mm, 250V 10A, 3.5mm, 7.4V 2200mAh, 4K60, 12MP).

Numeric size/capacity specifications in product-style text, especially hardware dimensions and equipment ratings expressed as a number followed by a unit or spec token (e.g., 120 mm, 25 mm, 12 kW, 50 liters, M8).

Alternative-size or converted-dimension expressions inside specs, especially side-by-side equivalent sizes such as imperial/metric restatements or close alternatives (e.g., 1/2 inch (13mm), 3/4\" or 19mm, 14 or 15mm).

The feature may be mildly polysemantic around average-report language in biomedical prose: strongest on literal statistical 'mean', but with secondary sensitivity to semantically related average-summary phrasing such as 'average' or 'on average' when reporting cohort measurements.

The feature activates on the word/phrase 'mean' used as a statistical average in biomedical/scientific results text, especially templates like 'The mean age was X', 'Mean surgical time was X', or 'a mean of X'.

A narrower variant: the feature prefers concise results/table-style summary-statistic templates where 'mean' appears adjacent to a study variable and a numeric value, often biomedical measurements and sometimes decimal or ± notation.
The feature strongly tracks the modal auxiliary token "would", especially when it follows an explicit subject in prose: patterns like "we would", "they would", "it would", "she would".

A particularly strong subfeature is polite/formal formulae with "would like to ...", especially acknowledgments, thanks, recognition, and similar academic or ceremonial prose (e.g. "we would like to thank/acknowledge...").
Another supported subcase is impersonal evaluative constructions using "would be", especially "it/that would be ..." and related rhetorical questions like "Would it/that not be ...".

Forum/tutorial prose introducing a Java code example, where the introduced snippet begins with a `package <java-style-name>;` declaration (e.g. 'I have the following class:' or 'the main class as follows:').

Java `package ...;` declaration shown as the first line of a displayed code snippet or file header, often immediately after prose like 'here is my class' or 'file begins' and often followed by `import` lines.
Java source-file header pattern specifically: `package <name>;` near the top of the file, often followed by blank lines and `import` statements.
Words for subnational or non-urban geographic regions, especially the tokens 'province/provinces', 'provincial', and 'rural'.
Location phrases that place something in or from a province or rural area, e.g. 'in the province', 'from the province', 'in rural areas/districts'.
Rural/provincial development or public-service contexts only when explicit region words are present (e.g. rural clinics, provincial schools, rural roads).

The feature primarily detects the literal token 'fast/Fast', especially when it functions as an adjective or as part of a fixed multiword expression/name (e.g. 'fast food', 'fast-paced', 'fast-flowing', 'Fast forward', 'Fast Track', 'Fast and Furious'). It is much less about the general concept of speed than about this specific lexical item in phrase-like contexts.

A strong subfeature is capitalized or phrase-initial 'Fast' in formulaic expressions, titles, and names, especially 'Fast forward ...' and title-like strings such as 'Fast and Furious', 'Fast Times', 'Fast Money', or 'Fast Forward'.

The feature prefers 'fast' as a modifier before a noun or inside hyphenated compounds (e.g. 'fast food', 'fast-track', 'fast-moving', 'fast-paced', 'fast-flowing'), with weaker activation for bare adverbial 'fast'.
South Slavic oblique personal pronoun forms built on nj- (njega, njemu, njoj, njih, nje), especially after prepositions, likely firing on an internal subtoken boundary within the pronoun.

Boundary feature for nonstandard pronoun-internal splits, especially English gender-inclusive slash forms like s/he and his/her, with possible secondary firing on tokenization boundaries inside South Slavic pronoun forms such as nje-ga / nje-mu / nje.

Token-boundary / segmentation feature for short pronoun-like forms containing an internal break marker, including slash-marked gender alternations (s/he, his/her) and tokenizer-induced internal splits in inflected pronouns such as njega/njemu/nje.

Android/Java import statements for UI-related classes specifically from `android.widget` (including widgets like `Button`, `ListView`, `TextView`, and likely `Toast`), rather than imports from other Android packages.

The fully qualified class-name pattern `android.widget.<Class>` for concrete Android UI/widget classes, with maximal activation when it appears in import-like Java code and weaker activation in other code-like mentions.

Java/Android import statements that import a specific class from the `android.widget` package, e.g. `import android.widget.Button;`, `import android.widget.ListView;`, `import android.widget.TextView;`.

Start of a C/C++ function declaration/definition with return type `void`, with strongest activation when `void` appears at the beginning of a new line and especially when separated from prior code by a just-closed block.

Lexical trigger on the token sequence of a brace/newline boundary into the keyword `void` in source code—i.e., the start of the next code unit after `}`—rather than semantic properties of the function itself.
Boilerplate warning/disclaimer language in technical text that forbids modification or reliance, especially generated-file notices like "DO NOT EDIT".
Interpersonal colloquial prohibitives using "don't" to head off an action by another person, especially verbs like ask/call/tell/email/text directed at "me" or the current speaker.
Negative imperative directives of the form "do not / don't + verb", especially commands addressed to the reader/listener forbidding an action (e.g. "do not edit", "don't ask me why", "don't touch").
The feature fires on the exact token/segment `openapi` when it appears as a package component in dotted Java/Kotlin-style names, especially IntelliJ references such as `com.intellij.openapi.*`.

Polysemantic feature with two concrete triggers: (1) the Python script guard `if __name__ == '__main__':` / `if __name__ == "__main__":`, and (2) the exact IntelliJ package segment `openapi` in dotted references like `com.intellij.openapi.*`.
The feature fires on the Python module-entry guard pattern `if __name__ == '__main__':`, centered on the `__main__` literal and tolerant to single vs double quotes around `__main__`.

Comma + 'with' introducing a non-argument supplementary clause that gives an accompanying state/process, often with a participial or predicative complement ('..., with bacteria being transmitted...', '..., with the extracellular side showing...').

Sentence-medial ', with ...' used to append contextual scene details or concurrent developments after a main clause, especially in expository/narrative prose ('The march continued, with banners snapping in the wind').
Comma + 'with' marking an absolute-like supplementary construction describing an accompanying state of a participant ('The child slept soundly, with one hand clutching a toy').

Genealogy-style appositive person descriptions combining a named individual with nearby kinship or identity metadata, often via commas or parentheses—e.g. 'Thomas, son of Edward and Anne' or 'Gladys (Oakwood) Sanders'.
Genealogical/biographical kinship phrasing centered on family relations in prose, especially templates like 'son/daughter of X and Y', 'wife of', 'mother of', or enumerations of children.
Parenthetical biographical inserts immediately after a personal name, especially genealogy-style metadata such as maiden names or birth notes: '(Oakwood)', '(née X)', '(born 1926)'.
The feature may extend to business/accounting terminology built around the word "cost," such as "cost centers," "cost allocation," "cost drivers," and related finance/operations phrases.
The feature activates on the token "cost" itself, especially noun uses in fixed patterns like "the cost of X," "cost to Y," or "at a cost," referring to expense, burden, or downside.
The feature is a broad lexical-semantic detector for mentions of cost/costs, including expense, tradeoff, burden, and business-cost terminology, rather than specifically evaluative decision contexts.

A complement-taking construction with nouns like 'chance', 'opportunity', or 'time' followed by 'to' or 'for', expressing an opening/availability for an action or event (e.g. 'chance to help', 'time for reflection').

More specifically, the feature strongly prefers the idiom of a favorable opening to act: 'chance to X' / 'opportunity to X', with possible extension to 'Now's your chance to...' and similar invitation/enabling frames.

A broader availability/enabling-noun + complement pattern may weakly activate the feature beyond 'chance/opportunity/time'—for example nouns like 'scope' or 'latitude' followed by 'for'/'to' complements—but this is secondary and inconsistent.
Genetics/chromosome inheritance terminology, especially sex-chromosome vs autosomal concepts such as heterogametic/homogametic, autosomes, sex-linked/X-linked, and chromosomal inheritance.

Scientific vocabulary about sex determination and chromosome-class distinctions, especially words like heterogametic, homogametic, autosomes, and sex chromosomes, rather than generic subword fragments such as 'game' or 'omes'.
A secondary sensitivity to compact cytogenetic locus notation and chromosome band references, such as 6p24.3, 9p21.3, 11q23, chr coordinates, and translocation notation.
The specific HTML boundary `attribute="value">`: the closing double quote immediately followed by `>`, marking the end of a start tag and transition into text/newline.

Closing double quote of a double-quoted HTML attribute value inside raw webpage markup, regardless of whether another attribute or the tag end follows; not quotes in prose, single-quoted attributes, or unquoted attributes.
An HTML double quote ending an attribute value, especially in real tag markup and often near tag termination (`">` or before another attribute/`>`).
Possible LaTeX-specific subfeature: opening parenthesis introduced by TeX-style constructs such as \left( or after decorated symbols/macros, rather than plain prose use of parentheses.

More specifically, it may respond to parenthesized arguments or qualifiers attached to a preceding math object—function/application syntax, matrix/operator arguments, or notation like H_0:(\mu=0), P(A|B), K(x,y).

The token is primarily detecting an opening parenthesis in math/LaTeX notation, especially immediately after a symbol or expression: f(x), R_i(R_j), K^{\rm ph}(T_c^{\rm ph}), \langle l|(, and \left( ...
